## What Works Well to Say

I've tried lots of different approaches and the honest answer is that what works one day won't always work the next as you need to read how your child is feeling.

### "How are you feeling?"
Simple, open, non-leading.

### "I loved watching you"
Not tied to outcome or performance.

### The comparison
"Jack was fantastic today, wasn't he - did you see the way he was driving forward?"

Comparisons with teammates are rarely as neutral as they feel to the parent saying them.

### The redirect to training
"We need to work on your shooting." "I think you need some extra sessions on your first touch."

### Processing your frustration out loud
"I thought the referee was awful." "The coach doesn't know what he's doing." "You should have played more."

## How grassroots football differs from academy football

The clearest way to separate the two is by purpose.

I should caveat that there are some grassroots teams that are more competitive that would still have trials and make selections.
- **Coaching structure:** grassroots coaching is volunteer-led and community-based, whereas academy coaching is delivered by paid, professionally qualified staff working to the club's own development curriculum.
- **Commitment:** grassroots training is typically once or twice a week plus a Saturday or Sunday match; academy training is generally more frequent, and structured against the club's own age-phase curriculum under the FA's [EPPP framework](/academy-pathway/what-is-eppp), which is worth reading if you want to understand exactly how that structure works rather than take the comparison on trust.
- **Security:** grassroots participation doesn't carry the risk of release.

## Touchline Behaviour

Sideline coaching is probably the most visible mistake youth football parents make, and it causes specific, concrete problems.
As I coach my son's team and also watch from the touchline as a parent with his other team, I've seen both sides of this.

In both roles, parent and coach, I've found one of the more powerful lines to just say 'stay involved' as often the biggest improvement in the younger ages is just getting them back focused after they have passed or when they don't have the ball.
One of the most common things I see as a coach is children looking towards the touchline before making a decision.
I remember one post game car journey saying to my son he should've shot more as he could've had a hatful if he'd shot quicker.
